problem: Source "You have a 'faux air' of Nebuchadnezzar in the fields about you" — 'faux air' means a slight or passing resemblance (something of the look of). MODERN "a distinct look of Nebuchadnezzar" makes it stronger than the playful hedge in the source.
new_text: "It's time someone undertook to bring you back to human shape," I said, parting his thick, long, uncut hair. "I see you're being turned into a lion, or something of the sort. You've got something of the look of Nebuchadnezzar out in the fields about you, that's certain—your hair reminds me of eagle feathers. Whether your nails have grown like bird claws, I haven't yet checked."

problem: Source "What do I sacrifice? Famine for food, expectation for content" means she gives up famine and gains food, gives up expectation and gains contentment. MODERN "Famine for food. Waiting for fulfillment." reads the second item as one noun phrase ('waiting for fulfillment'), so the exchange is lost and it sounds as if she sacrifices fulfillment.
new_text: "Sacrifice! What do I sacrifice? I trade famine for food, and suspense for contentment. To be allowed to put my arms around what I treasure—to press my lips to what I love—to rest against what I trust: is that a sacrifice? If so, then yes—I delight in sacrifice."
